Revelation is the final book of the New Testament, a visionary apocalyptic text attributed to John the Apostle. It describes end-times prophecies, cosmic battles, and divine judgment. It is frequently confused with other apocalyptic or mystical Christian texts, and its symbols are often misinterpreted in popular culture.

Revelation was written in the late first century of the common era, likely during persecution of early Christians under Roman rule. The visions address the suffering church's hope for vindication. It is not the only apocalyptic text in the Bible. The book of Daniel, parts of Matthew, and the first Epistle to the Thessalonians also contain eschatological material. But Revelation is the only canonical Christian apocalypse.

The Four Horsemen appear in Revelation chapter six. They represent Conquest, War, Famine, and Death. This passage is not from Ezekiel or other prophetic books, though Ezekiel does have visions of wheels and thrones. The famous number 666 appears in Revelation 13:18 and refers to a specific beast. It was likely a coded reference to Nero Caesar in gematria, an ancient Hebrew system of numerical substitution. The number is not a universal symbol of evil outside that specific chapter.

The Rapture—the sudden taking away of believers before tribulation—is not explicitly named in Revelation. The concept is primarily drawn from the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter four, verse seventeen. Millennialism, the thousand-year reign described in Revelation chapter twenty, has produced three major Christian interpretive traditions: premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial. Each tradition reads the same text differently.
